reviews.question: If a particle is in static equilibrium, then the work done by the system of forces acting on that particle is:
reviews.explanation: Static equilibrium is a state in which the net force and net torque on the system are zero. The linear and angular momenta are consequently constant; for a particle in static equilibrium it remains at rest. Since its actual displacement is zero, the work done by the acting force system is zero.
reviews.note: Keyc verified. The full printed equilibrium/momentum explanation is retained and connected explicitly to zero displacement.

reviews.question: A 500 N block is moved upward 1.6 m along a plane inclined 45° to horizontal. What is the work done by the applied force?(Friction coefficient μ=0.25.)

reviews.question: The potential energy an elevator losses in coming down from the top of a building to stop at the ground floor is

options.c: lost in friction of the moving surfaces
options.d: used up in lifting the counter poise weight

reviews.explanation: In a counterweighted elevator, the descending car can transfer gravitational potential energy into raising the counterweight. In general the balance also includes motor electrical work or regeneration, friction and braking heat. The car and counterweight masses and drive/braking conditions are not specified, so it is not generally true that the car’s entire lost potential energy is used solely to lift the counterweight. Option(d) is a possible contribution under an idealized balance, not a complete unique general answer.

reviews.question: A man is pulling a bucket of water up to the roof of a building of 6 m height. The total weight of the rope is 20 N and the weight of the bucket with water is 100 N. The work done by the man is
reviews.explanation: Given h=6 m, rope weight mg=20 N, and bucket-plus-water weight Mg=100 N. Work equals the increase in gravitational potential energy of the bucket and rope. A uniform rope initially hanging through 6 m has its centre of mass h/2=6/2=3 m below the roof. Hence W_work=Mgh+mg(h/2)=(M+m/2)gh=(Mg+mg/2)h=(100+20/2)×6=660 N·m.
reviews.note: Uniform rope is implicit in the source centre-of-mass calculation.600 J raises bucket; 60 J raises rope.

reviews.question: According to the Principle of ‘Virtual Work', which quantity remains zero during the analysis?

options.a: Virtual displacement due to external force
options.b: External force due to virtual work
options.c: External work due to real displacement

reviews.explanation: Principle of virtual work: if the forces acting on a body or system of bodies are in equilibrium, and the system is imagined to undergo a small displacement consistent with its geometrical constraints, then the algebraic sum of virtual work of all forces is zero. Thus the total work due to admissible virtual displacement is zero, not each individual force’s work.
reviews.note: Full printed principle retained; emphasized total sum and equilibrium/constraint conditions.

reviews.question: Virtual work means 1. work done by real forces due to virtual displacement 2. work done by virtual forces during real displacement
reviews.explanation: The source gives two dual forms: virtual work=virtual force×real displacement, or virtual work=virtual displacement×real force. In vector notation these are work pairingsδF·u and F·δu. The usual virtual-displacement principle uses actual forces and kinematically admissible virtual displacements. The complementary virtual-force principle uses equilibrated virtual forces/stresses with actual compatible displacements. Thus both listed descriptions are recognized in these dual formulations.
reviews.note: Both 1 and 2 verified with the distinction between standard and complementary virtual-work principles.

reviews.question: A lifting machine will be reversible, if the efficiency
reviews.explanation: A reversible lifting machine can do work in the reverse direction after the effort is removed; the lifted load then descends. In the conventional lifting-machine friction-work model, the load’s released potential energy must exceed the frictional loss. The limiting equality gives 50% efficiency, so the reversible condition isη>50%, choice(a).
reviews.note: General threshold choice a is intended; 100% or>75% are more restrictive sufficient cases, not the threshold criterion.

reviews.explanation: For a smooth ideal pulley with the 600 N block in equilibrium, the rope tension isT=600 N. The upward rope force on the man reduces the normal force at his feet. Floor balance gives N=man’s weight−T=800−600=200 N. He presses the floor with the same 200 N magnitude.

reviews.question: For the illustrated unstable equilibrium at a potential-energy maximum, the potential energy _____ on a small virtual displacement away from equilibrium.
reviews.explanation: For one-dimensional conservative equilibrium, U′=0. The source illustrates three cases: (1)Stable equilibrium is a local minimum of U; for a nondegenerate minimum U″>0, and sufficiently small departures raise U.(2)Unstable equilibrium at a local maximum has U″<0 in the nondegenerate case, and departures lower U, so choice(a)applies.(3)Neutral equilibrium requires U to remain constant throughout the nearby allowed configurations, so such displacements leave U unchanged and U″=0 there. The equality U″=0 at a single point alone does not prove neutrality: U=x⁴ has U″(0)=0 but a stable minimum. In systems with several degrees of freedom, an unstable saddle need only have an energy-lowering direction, not a maximum in every direction.
reviews.note: Retained key a and all three source cases; corrected the implication that U″=0 alone proves neutral equilibrium and stated the illustrated one-dimensional maximum condition.

Neutral condition: body has constant potential energyU; d²U/dx²=0; for any virtual displacement U is unchanged.

reviews.explanation: In a track-type machine, the front idler and yoke guide the track chain and preserve its alignment, so(a)is the intended direct function. Active tension adjustment depends on the associated adjuster/recoil arrangement.

reviews.question: In a lock gate, the reaction between its two leaves is what? P is the resultant hydrostatic force on one leaf, and α is its inclination to the normal to the side of the lock.
reviews.explanation: For symmetric miter gates, the hydrostatic resultantP on one leaf acts at its midpoint along the leaf’s width. Taking moments about that leaf’s wall hinge gives P(L/2)=R L sin α, whereR is the contact reaction between leaves and α is the stated gate inclination from the normal to the lock side. Therefore R=P/(2 sin α). The complete printed explanation consists of this formula.
reviews.note: Keya independently verified by hinge-moment equilibrium for the standard symmetric miter-gate geometry.

reviews.question: In lifting machines, as load increases the mechanical advantage
reviews.explanation: Lifting machines apply effort at one point and lift the load at another. In the stated ordinary law-of-machine model P=mW+C, with C>0, the mechanical advantage is MA=W/P=W/(mW+C)=1/(m+C/W). As W increases, C/W decreases and MA increases, approaching 1/m. This verifies the source’s statement that increasing load increases mechanical advantage for this model; an ideal C=0 machine instead has constant MA.

reviews.question: The velocity ratio as per law of machine equals which expression?(The source defines m as the line slope and says it equals the coefficient of friction; W is load and C the effort needed to overcome friction.)
reviews.explanation: The law of machine is P=mW+C. Dividing by W gives P/W=m+C/W=1/MA. This is an effort-to-load ratio, not velocity ratio. VR is the ratio of effort displacement to load displacement and is normally fixed by machine geometry. Neither the law alone nor the listed expressions determine it. Also m is the empirical slope of the effort–load line; it is not generally the material coefficient of friction. Thus the printed(a)formula has been assigned the wrong quantity and the item must remain ungraded.
reviews.note: Full source explanation is at top printed p 130. Formula is P/W=1/MA, not VR; the slope is not generally a friction coefficient.
